concept.title: Securing the Impala Web User Interface

conbody.p:
The instructions in this section presume you are familiar with the
.htpasswd mechanism commonly used to password-protect pages on web servers.

Password-protect the Impala web UI that listens on port 25000 by default. Set up a .htpasswd file in the $IMPALA_HOME directory, or start both the impalad and statestored daemons with the --webserver_password_file option to specify a different location (including the filename).

This file should only be readable by the Impala process and machine administrators, because it contains (hashed) versions of passwords. The username / password pairs are not derived from Unix usernames, Kerberos users, or any other system. The domain field in the password file must match the domain supplied to Impala by the new command-line option --webserver_authentication_domain. The default is mydomain.com.

Impala also supports using HTTPS for secure web traffic. To do so, set --webserver_certificate_file to refer to a valid .pem TLS/SSL certificate file. Impala will automatically start using HTTPS once the TLS/SSL certificate has been read and validated. A .pem file is basically a private key, followed by a signed TLS/SSL certificate; make sure to concatenate both parts when constructing the .pem file.
If Impala cannot find or parse the .pem file, it prints an error message and quits.

note.p: If the private key is encrypted using a passphrase, Impala will ask for that passphrase on startup, which is not useful for a large cluster. In that case, remove the passphrase and make the .pem file readable only by Impala and administrators.
When you turn on TLS/SSL for the Impala web UI, the associated URLs change from http:// prefixes to https://. Adjust any bookmarks or application code that refers to those URLs.

concept.title: SAML2 Single Sign-On for the Web UI

conbody.p: Starting in , the coordinator Web UI supports SAML2 single sign-on. When a user opens a page of the Web UI without being authenticated, Impala redirects the browser to the IdP. After the user signs in, Impala sets an authentication cookie and redirects the browser to the page that the user requested. Impala preserves the original URI in the SAML RelayState.
Register Impala at the IdP and configure the shared flags as described in . In addition, set the following flags on the coordinators:

ul.li: --webserver_saml2_idp_metadata: The path of the metadata file of the IdP.

--webserver_saml2_sp_callback_url: The URL where the IdP posts the SAML responses, in the form https://host:port/path. Use the port of the Web UI as the browser reaches it, which is --webserver_port unless a proxy maps a different port. Setting this flag turns on SAML2 for the Web UI.
SAML2 applies to the Web UI of the impalad daemons that run as coordinators (--is_coordinator=true).
The Web UI must use TLS (--webserver_certificate_file).
You cannot use --webserver_password_file together with SAML2.
The Web UI must use authentication cookies, so --max_cookie_lifetime_s must be greater than 0. The default value is 86400 seconds (1 day).

Impala keeps the state of a sign-in in the memory of the coordinator for 5 minutes, so the user must finish the sign-in in that time, and the IdP must post the response to the coordinator that started the sign-in.

conbody.p: You can combine SAML2 with the Kerberos (SPNEGO) and LDAP authentication of the Web UI. A request that has no Authorization header goes to SAML2. If the client sends Kerberos or LDAP credentials and they are not valid, Impala returns the HTTP status 401 and does not use SAML2.

The authentication cookie is controlled by the same flags as the cookies of the HiveServer2 HTTP endpoint: --max_cookie_lifetime_s sets its lifetime, and --cookie_secret_file makes the cookies of several coordinators valid on each other. See .
The metrics impala.webserver.total-saml-auth-success and impala.webserver.total-saml-auth-failure count the successful and failed authentications.
